overview:
Four Soviet republics signed a union treaty on 30 December 1922, formalising a state that had already been assembled in fact by the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War. What emerged over the following decades was the largest country on earth — some 22.4 million square kilometres, eventually fifteen republics, roughly 287 million people at the 1989 census — governed by a single party whose ideology claimed to be a universal science of history rather than a national programme. Lenin's New Economic Policy allowed a partial retreat to markets in the 1920s; after his death in 1924 and the manoeuvring that left Stalin dominant, the state turned to forced collectivisation of agriculture and crash industrialisation. That decade produced both the heavy industry that would later stop the Wehrmacht and a famine in 1932–33 that killed millions, most heavily in Ukraine and Kazakhstan, followed by the mass arrests, deportations and executions of the Great Terror in 1937–38.

The war remade the country's place in the world and its sense of itself. After the 1939 pact with Nazi Germany and the German invasion of June 1941, the USSR absorbed the largest share of the fighting in Europe and lost around 27 million people, more than any other combatant. Victory brought control over eastern Europe, a nuclear arsenal by 1949, and forty years of confrontation with the United States that ran through Berlin, Korea, Cuba and a long list of proxy wars. It also brought genuine prestige: Sputnik in 1957 and Gagarin's flight in 1961 made the Soviet model look, for a moment, like the future. Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin in 1956 loosened the terror without dismantling the system; under Brezhnev after 1964 the state grew stable, heavily armed and economically sclerotic, a period Soviet citizens themselves later called stagnation.

The end came quickly and largely from within. The Afghan war begun in 1979, the Chernobyl disaster of 1986, and an economy that could not deliver consumer goods or absorb falling oil revenues all pressed on a leadership that had run out of answers. Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost after 1985 were meant to repair the system; instead they licensed criticism the party could not contain and gave the national movements in the Baltics, the Caucasus and Ukraine room to organise. A hardline coup against Gorbachev in August 1991 collapsed in three days and destroyed what authority the centre had left. In December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared the union dissolved; Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin on 25 December 1991.
significance: For most of the twentieth century the Soviet Union was the principal alternative to liberal capitalism, and almost nothing in that century is legible without it — the defeat of Nazi Germany, the shape of decolonisation, the terms on which anticolonial and labour movements everywhere argued about development, the nuclear standoff that organised world politics for forty years. Its collapse left fifteen successor states, an unresolved question of borders and minorities that still produces war, and a lasting argument about whether the system failed because of its ideology, its economics, or the particular men who ran it. It also stands as the most sustained attempt ever made to remake a society by state power, and the human cost of that attempt remains one of the central moral facts of modern history.
coverage: This was written from general reference works rather than the specialist literature, and the dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date. Two caveats about the record itself: for most of the Soviet period the only detailed documentation was produced by the state that was doing the killing, and the archives that opened after 1991 were never fully opened — Foreign Ministry, KGB and presidential holdings remain largely closed, and access has tightened again since. Death tolls for the 1932–33 famine and the Terror are therefore estimates with wide ranges, and whether the Ukrainian famine constitutes genocide is genuinely contested among historians, not settled.
